title: Motion that helps, and motion that makes people leave
excerpt: Website animation best practices come down to one test: motion should show a relationship or a state. Looping decoration that fights reading should go.
alt: A close view of a smartphone home screen filled with app icons on a pale table. The phone fills the frame the way a visitor actually meets motion, in the hand.
caption: Motion is judged on a phone, in the hand, not in a reel. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: When is animation worth keeping?
faqs.answer: When it shows where something came from, or that a state changed. A menu that opens from the button you tapped, or a save that visibly confirms, helps. A background that loops forever, a custom cursor, or an intro that delays the headline does not. If you cannot say what the motion explains, remove it.

faqs.question: Can animation hurt more than taste?
faqs.answer: Yes. Motion that shifts layout after load adds to Cumulative Layout Shift, which web.dev wants at 0.1 or less for a good score. Motion that keeps the main thread busy makes taps feel late. The person experiences both as the site fighting them, even if the storyboard looked smooth on a laptop.

faqs.question: What is Hanabi's rule for reduced motion?
faqs.answer: The page has to work when motion is reduced. Decorative movement should stop or simplify when a person has asked their system for less motion. Information should not live only inside an animation. The still page is part of done, not a degraded extra.

markdown:
Website animation best practices fit in one test. Motion should show a relationship or a state. It should tell you where a panel came from, or that something changed because you acted. Looping decoration that fights reading should go. So should any move that has to finish before a person is allowed to read the offer.

A visitor does not grade your reel. They try to do a job: understand the company, or start a conversation. Motion that helps that job can stay. Motion that delays it, distracts from it, or makes the page jump is the reason people leave, even when they cannot name the animation as the cause.

## Motion that shows a relationship

Relationship means the person can see that this thing and that thing are connected. A menu opens from the button that asked for it. A dialog sits above the page that opened it, and closes back to that page. A new section does not appear from nowhere if a short move can show that it was the next step.

These moves are short. They are causally obvious. They do not loop. When they end, the page is a normal page again, and the person can read. If the move is so slow that reading waits on it, it is no longer explaining. It is withholding.

Hanabi uses a motion library where a transition earns its place, and keeps the marketing site visually stable. The standard is reduced motion as part of the craft, not as a patch. If a relationship can be shown by layout alone, layout is enough. A well-placed panel does not need to fly in from the edge of the screen to be understood.

## Motion that shows a state

State means the system heard the person. A button acknowledges a press. A save goes from idle to done. A field shows an error at the moment of the error, not ten seconds later with no connection to the action. A small change in the control is often the whole animation.

This is the motion people miss when it is absent, even if they never praise it when it is present. A form that sits there after a click feels broken. A form that confirms feels finished. You do not need a mascot, a confetti burst, or a full-screen transition to deliver that feeling. You need a visible response.

Keep state motion on the object that changed. Animating the entire page because one toggle flipped is how a tool becomes tiring for someone who uses it every day. Marketing pages get more leeway than a product someone lives in, and still less leeway than a showreel.

## Motion that makes people leave

Intro sequences that play before the headline. Parallax that lags the text behind the scroll. Cursors that replace the one the system already draws. Background videos that say nothing the poster frame did not say. Carousels that move the proof while someone is trying to read it.

These share a trait. They ask for attention the page has not earned, and they keep asking. A person who wanted the price, the offer, or the login now has a second job: waiting out the decoration. Some of them will wait. Many will not. You will not get a note about why.

There is a measured version of the same problem. [web.dev](https://web.dev/articles/vitals) defines Cumulative Layout Shift as the visual stability metric, and a good score is 0.1 or less. Animation that pushes content around after load, or that reserves no space for the thing it is about to reveal, adds to that score. The page moves under a finger. The person misses the button. Taste is not a defense.

The W3C's [WCAG 2 overview](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/) frames the deeper issue. The guidelines exist so web content is more accessible, under principles that include perceivable and operable. If the only explanation of a change is a move, the change is invisible to someone who does not track motion well, and it is hostile to someone who asked their system to reduce it. Put the meaning in the text and the layout. Let motion repeat the meaning, not replace it.

## A way to review a storyboard

Take each move in the storyboard and write the sentence it is for. This shows the menu belongs to that button. This confirms the message sent. If the sentence is this feels premium, cut the move. Premium is not a relationship or a state. It is a mood you are hoping will arrive if enough things drift.

Then play the page with motion off. If it looks broken, the design was hiding in the animation. Rebuild the still page until it is complete. Add back only the moves whose sentences you kept. Check them on a phone, because a sweep that feels graceful on a 27-inch display often feels like a delay in the hand.

Time-box the ones you keep. A transition that takes most of a second will be felt as lag the tenth time, even if it felt cinematic the first. State changes should be faster than the person can wonder whether the tap worked. Relationship changes should be fast enough that the reading does not pause.

## What Hanabi refuses

The studio's public standard is clarity over complexity, with reduced motion treated as part of done. That means a looping hero is a hard sell. It means an entrance that gates the headline does not ship. It means the page someone gets when they prefer less motion is designed, not merely the animated page with the keyframes deleted until it looks accidental.

You can still have a point of view. A calm brand moves rarely and quietly. A denser product moves only to confirm. A single well-made transition can be a signature if the rest of the page is still. The signature is recognizable because it is scarce.

The reduced-motion version is its own piece of craft, not a footnote. [Reduced motion is part of the craft](/blog/reduced-motion) is the next article, about shipping two versions of a move on purpose.

When you want motion held to that test on a real site, see [Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services). The useful animation is the one you can justify in a sentence, and remove without losing the meaning.
